title: ATIBIR INDUSTRIES CO. LTD VS. STATE BANK OF INDIA

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1156
Page 1 of 31
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL Nos. OF 2026
@ SLP (C) Nos. 21029-30 OF 2024
ATIBIR INDUSTRIES CO. LTD. ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE BANK OF INDIA & ANR. ...RESPONDENTS
J U D G M E N T
V. MOHANA, J.
1. Leave Granted.
2. The present Appeals arise out of a common judgment and order dated
25.07.2024 passed by the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in APO
No.180 of 2023 and APOT No.393 of 2023 filed by the Respondents herein.
3. The Appellant, a borrower of the consortium of banks led by the
Respondent No.1, had challenged the classification of its loan account as a
Non-Performing Asset and its subsequent assignment by Respondent No.1 in
favour of the Respondent No.2 which is an asset reconstruction company.

Page 2 of 31
4. The Appellant is engaged in the business of manufacturing sponge iron,
pig iron and allied products. It availed various credit facilities including cash
credit, term loans and letters of credit from a consortium of banks led by
Respondent No.1. The credit facilities were secured by hypothecation of the
Appellant's current assets, ranking pari passu with the other consortium banks
and of its plant and machinery; by equitable mortgages, also ranking pari passu
over its factory land and buildings and over leasehold factory land and
commercial plots owned by two group companies; and by the personal
guarantees of five of its promoters and the corporate guarantees of those two
companies.
5. The Respondent No.1, by letters dated 18.01.2019 and 17.03.2020,
informed the Appellant of the devolvement of bills under foreign and domestic
letters of credit and requested the debtor to regularise its loan account and
submit a cash budget covering at least until June, 2020. By letter dated
17.01.2020, the Appellant informed the Respondent No.1 of its inability to pay
the dues and undertook to regularise the account by 22.01.2020. Thereafter,
the Appellant submitted resolution plans to the Respondent No.1 including the
revised plan dated 11.06.2020 in which it acknowledged that as against a
sanctioned limit of Rs.155 crores, the outstanding cash credit was Rs.278.56
crores as on 31.03.2020 and which became Rs.302 crores as on 06.06.2020.
The Appellant attributed its default to several factors including the COVID-19

Page 3 of 31
pandemic, and relied upon three circulars dated 27.03.2020, 17.04.2020 and
23.05.2020 issued by the Reserve Bank of India (for short the "RBI") under
which the RBI extended the moratorium on repayment up to 31.08.2020. By a
letter dated 15.09.2020, the Respondent No.1 revised the term loan repayment
schedule, fixing the first instalment on 30.09.2020. The Appellant, thereafter,
paid Rs.21,07,157/- on 01.11.2020 and Rs.80 lakhs on 11.12.2020.
6. By a letter dated 05.04.2021, Respondent No.1 informed the Appellant
that its account had been irregular since 17.01.2020; that the Supreme Court
vide judgment dated 23.03.2021 in Small Scale Industrial Manufacturers
Association v. Union of India1 had lifted the blanket ban on classification of
accounts as NPA; and that the account of the Appellant had been classified as
NPA on 31.03.2021 with effect from 16.10.2020. The letter also sets out the
dues of the Appellant as Rs.310.46 crores in the cash credit account and seven
working capital loan accounts, Rs.16 crores in the term loan account and
Rs.27.05 crores in four funded interest term loan accounts. The Respondent
No.1 demanded that the Appellant should clear the overdues or submit a
comprehensive resolution plan.
1
(2021) 8 SCC 511

Page 4 of 31
7. On 17.01.2022, the Respondent No.1 issued a recall notice demanding
Rs.341 crores by way of principal along with accrued interest and other charges
from the Appellant. The Respondent No.1 also approached the Debts Recovery
Tribunal-I, Kolkata, by instituting OA No.260 of 2022 under Section 19 of the
Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 to recover a sum of
Rs.396,36,17,844.
8. In the meantime, the Respondent No.1 also filed a petition under Section
7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (for short the "IBC") before
the National Company Law Tribunal, Kolkata (for short the "NCLT") seeking
initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process against the Appellant (for
short the "NCLT Proceedings").
9. The Appellant proposed one-time settlement to the Respondent No.1
through its letters dated 25.01.2022, 27.01.2022, 28.02.2022 and 23.05.2022.
The offer was increased from Rs.227 crores to Rs.237 crores, none of which
was accepted by the Respondent No.1. The final offer was revised to Rs.238
crores on 07.02.2023. The Appellant paid about Rs.25 crores to the Respondent
No.1 from time to time between 06.02.2021 and 25.01.2023.
10. On 08.07.2022, the Respondent No.1 issued a notice under Section 13(2)
of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement
of Security Interest Act, 2002 (for short the "SARFAESI Act") recording the
default and the classification of the Appellant's account as a Non-Performing

Page 5 of 31
Asset as on 16.10.2020, and directed the Appellant to pay Rs.410,26,78,340/-
along with further interest, incidental expenses and costs. The Appellant did
not respond to the above notice. On 28.10.2022, the Respondent No.1 issued a
notice under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act which was recalled by a
subsequent notice dated 04.11.2022.
11. After withdrawing the notice under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act,
the Respondent No.1 issued a web notice dated 10.02.2023 classifying the loan
account of the Appellant as a stressed loan exposure and placing it for transfer
to eligible asset reconstruction companies, banks and financial institutions
through e-auction. The Appellant challenged the said notice dated 10.02.2023
before the High Court by filing WPO No.428 of 2023 in which the learned
Single Judge granted an interim order dated 06.03.2023 directing the deferment
of the e-auction. Subsequently, the writ petition was withdrawn by the
Appellant on 21.03.2023 with liberty to file a fresh writ petition. On
23.03.2023, the Respondent No.1 issued a corrigendum advancing the e-auction process of the stressed loan exposure to 24.03.2023. The Appellant on
24.03.2023 filed WPO No.722 of 2023 seeking cancellation of the web notice
dated 10.02.2023, corrigendum dated 23.03.2023 and challenging the
classification of its account as a Non-Performing Asset. It contended that the
classification was contrary to the master circular on asset classification and the
COVID-19 relief circular issued by the RBI.

Page 6 of 31
PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE HIGH COURT: -
12. During the pendency of the writ, Respondent No.1 assigned the loan to
Respondent No.2 under an assignment agreement (for short the "Assignment
Agreement") on 24.03.2023 for a consideration of Rs.250 crores.
13. Before the learned Single Judge, the Petitioners challenged that the
classification of the Petitioner's account as NPA was palpably de hors the
relevant circular issued by the RBI during the pandemic period. It was
submitted that in terms of several RBI circulars extending the benefit of
moratorium to all debtors during the COVID-19 period, the Petitioner was
exonerated from paying any amount to the Respondent No.1 till 30.11.2023;
that the circulars dated 27.03.2020, 17.04.2020 and 23.05.2020 extended the
moratorium till 31.08.2020; that the cumulative effect would be that the
Appellant was exempted from paying the installments of the term loans till
30.11.2020, therefore, the default would have commenced only from
01.12.2020 and, hence the account of the Appellant could not have been
classified as NPA on 16.10.2020.
14. It was submitted that even otherwise the revised repayment schedule
dated 15.09.2020 exonerated the Appellant from paying any amount to the
Respondent No.1 till 30.09.2020 when the Appellant was required to pay an
amount of Rs.80 lakhs only. It was contended that the account could be
classified as NPA only if interest and/or installment of the principal remains

Page 7 of 31
overdue for a period of more than 90 days in respect of a term loan. Even
assuming for the sake of argument, the account was running irregular from
January, as per IRAC norms, 90 days of default was required to classify an
account as NPA. The Appellant further contended that the loan could not have
been branded as a stressed loan exposure and, therefore, it could not have been
placed for transfer to an asset loan reconstruction company. It was further
contended that the OTS proposals offered by the Appellant were not considered
and it was dealt with in a perfunctory manner. The Respondent No.1 contended
that the asset was declared as NPA and no steps were taken by the Appellant to
challenge the classification and that the bank can transfer even when loans are
not in default and not stressed loans. The Respondent No.2 submitted before
the High Court that a bank decides to assign its stressed loan exposure in
accordance with the decision taken by the banks as per their commercial
wisdom and that restructuring of stressed loans and management of Non-Performing Asset are commercial matters which should be left to the expertise
of large nationalised bank like the State Bank of India and that a defaulting
borrower has no locus to undo an assignment in favour of the asset
reconstruction company while in default of more than Rs.342 crores. The
learned Single Judge, while examining all the issues, came to the conclusion
that the Appellant was justified in arguing that the due date of repayment was
shifted across the board till after 31.08.2020. The learned Single Judge held
that in view of the moratorium having been extended till 31.08.2020, the due

Page 8 of 31
date for the purpose of marking the account overdue was shifted till 01.09.2020
and, therefore, to classify an account as NPA, the bank had to wait for 90 days
thereafter, in terms of the 2015 circular. Hence, it was held that the
classification of the account of the Appellant as NPA with effect from
16.10.2020 was premature and clearly in contravention of the RBI Master
Circular dated 01.07.2015 read with the pandemic circular issued by the RBI
and, therefore, the declaration that the account was NPA was set aside. As a
consequence, the Single Judge set aside the assignment of the debt to the
Respondent No.2 since the account is not a stressed loan which could be
transferred to an asset reconstruction company and allowed the Writ Petition
WPO No.722 of 2023 setting aside the classification of the Appellant's term
loan account with the Respondent No.1 as NPA with effect from 16.10.2020
and consequentially the web notice dated 10.02.2023 issued by the Respondent
No.1 for e-auction of the loan account of the Appellant as also the corrigenda
issued by the Respondent No.1. All actions taken in pursuance of the same
were quashed and reversed.
15. Aggrieved by the judgment of the learned Single Judge, two Appeals
were filed before the Division Bench of High Court by the Respondent Nos.1
and 2 herein respectively. The Division Bench by its impugned judgment dated
25.07.2024 allowed both the Appeals. The Division Bench held that the
classification of any of the credit facilities as NPA would affect the borrower

Page 9 of 31
across the spectrum of credit facilities enjoyed, as the asset classification must
be borrower-wise and not account-wise. Though this argument was not taken
by the Respondents before the learned Single Judge, the Division Bench took
the above submissions of the Respondents and held that since the account of
the Appellant had become stressed asset because of default in the cash credit
account, his term loan account can also be classified as NPA though it may not
have been NPA. The Division Bench held that assuming that the
borrower/Appellant may claim the benefit of doubt concerning the
classification of the term loan account as NPA, even then, the account of the
Appellant so far as the cash credit facilities are concerned turn NPA and,
therefore, the account was correctly classified as NPA by the Respondent No.1.
It further held that the Respondent No.1 could proceed under Section 5 of the
SARFAESI Act and sell the financial asset upon such financial asset becoming
NPA or Special Mention Account (for short the "SMA") before the date of sale.
Though, under the SARFAESI Act the bank had issued a notice under Section
13(2) and there was a mechanism subsequently which had to be followed under
Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, if the borrower fails to discharge the
liability, the Respondent No.1, in this case, had chosen to sell its financial assets
under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act and, therefore, it is not a measure
contemplated under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act. The Division Bench
held that the date on which the account should be considered as NPA or not for
a sale under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act, in the facts of the case, would be

Page 10 of 31
the date of publication of the web notice and it need not be pinned to the date
of NPA mentioned in the notice under Section 13(2). Hence, the Division
Bench held that the act of assignment or the process to assign the financial asset
does not violate any right of the borrower. On the issue of whether the cash
credit account having becoming NPA could be taken to declare the entire credit
facility as NPA, the Division Bench held that such an issue, though not raised
before the learned Single Judge, can be permitted to be raised for the first time
in the Appeal. The Division Bench held that the Respondent No.1-bank has
proceeded under Section 5 of the SARFAESI Act and not under Section 13(4)
thereof and in any event the Appellant-borrower has failed to discharge the
burden of rebutting the presumption that the account became NPA on the date
of the web notice which is 10.02.2023 and held that the Respondent No.1 has
acted in the manner recognized by law and, hence, allowed the Appeals filed
by the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 and dismissed the WPO No.722 of 2023.
Hence, the Appeals by the Appellant.
PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THIS COURT: -
16. When the matter was first taken up by this Court on 17.09.2024, the
Appellant was granted the short time to get instructions regarding the discharge
of the substantial part of the loan liability within a short time. Subsequent to
that, by an order dated 20.09.2024 a proposal was placed by the Appellant
before this Court to discharge the liability of Rs.250 crores in a time bound

Page 11 of 31
manner. The relevant portion of order dated 20.09.2024 of this Court reads
thus:-
"2. In compliance with the order dated 17.09.2024, the learned Senior
Counsel for the petitioner has placed on record the following proposal:
"(i) Upfront payment on or before September 25, 2024 :- Rs 25
Crores
(ii) On or before October 31, 2024 : - Rs. 50 Crores
(iii) On or before November 30, 2024 : - Rs. 50 Crores
(iv) On or before December 31, 2024 : - Rs. 50 Crores
(v) On or before January 31, 2025 : - Rs. 50 Crores
(vi) On or before February 28, 2025 : - Rs. 25 Crores"
3. As there this is a dispute concerning the total liability of the petitioner-Company, we find that except the offer of total amount of Rs.250 crores
by the petitioner, the rest of the proposal, being just and fair, can be
accepted to save the running industry. Regarding the total liability of the
petitioner, the same can be determined by a judicial/quasi-judicial forum,
subject to further intervention by this Court. S/Shri Dr. Abhishek Mani
Singhvi and Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel for respondent No.2
seek one week to obtain instructions in this regard.
4. Post these matters for further consideration on 27.09.2024.
5. The petitioner shall bring a cheque of Rs.25 crores on the date fixed.
6. The parties shall maintain status quo, as it exists today, till the next
date of hearing."
17. This Court, after considering the schedule, passed an order whereby the
offer of this total amount of Rs.25 crores and the rest of the proposal being just
and fair, in order to save the running industry of the Appellant suggested a
proposal that a quasi-judicial forum or the judicial forum can be directed to
quantify the further liability and, therefore, directed the parties to seek

Page 12 of 31
instructions in that regard. During the subsequent hearings dated 27.09.2024,
04.11.2024 and 14.10.2024, certain amounts have been paid in terms of the
undertaking by the Appellant to the Respondent No.2. On 09.12.2024, this
Court passed the following order:-
"1. Vide paragraph 2 of the order dated 20.09.2024, a schedule for
payment of Rs.250 crores by the petitioner-Company to the respondent
was laid down. As there was some dispute with regard to the total liability
of the petitioner-Company over and above Rs. 250 crores, it was
suggested that let such liability, if any, of the petitioner-Company be
determined by a judicial or quasi-judicial forum, of course, subject to
final approval by this Court.
2. Learned senior counsel for the parties jointly state that the third
installment of Rs.50 crores, which was payable by 30.11.2024 has also
been paid by the petitioner-Company.
3. Adverting to the suggestion given by Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi,
learned senior counsel and in deference to paragraph 3 of the above-mentioned order dated 20.09.2024, we resolve to appoint Hon'ble Mr.
Justice Anil R. Dave, former Judge of this Court, to adjudicate the claim
for interest and/or any other liability over and above Rs. 250 crores.
4. We request Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave to permit the parties to
submit their claims in writing in this regard and thereafter accord one
opportunity of oral submissions to them.
5. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of this case, we request
Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave to give his report at the earliest, subject
to His Lordship's convenience.
6. We are consciously not illustrating the issues that may be determined
by Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave, as we leave it to the parties to raise
all such issues for determination.
7. We request Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave to determine his own
fee, which shall be payable by the petitioner-Company.
8. Learned counsel for the parties may approach Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil
R. Dave along with copy of this order."
18. On 27.01.2025, this Court perused the proceedings held before Hon'ble
Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave on 02.01.2025 and found that he had not been able to

Page 13 of 31
proceed with the hearings owing to the delay on the part of the Respondent
No.2 in filing its claim. On the undertaking that the Respondent No.2 would
extend full cooperation, this Court requested Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave
to take up the matter on priority basis and to submit the report at the earliest.
This Court also took note of the failure of the Appellant in adhering to the
payment schedule and recorded that the instalments at serial Nos.1, 2 and 3 of
the order dated 20.09.2024 have been paid but there has been a default in
respect of serial No.4, and instalment at serial No.5 had fallen due. The Court
recorded the fact that the Appellant had handed over cheques for Rs.10 crores
to the Respondent No.2 which was accepted without prejudice to the rights of
the parties to seek further payment as per the schedule. By subsequent orders
dated 28.02.2025, 21.03.2025 and 16.05.2025 further payments were recorded
and on 15.07.2025, and it was noted that Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave had
submitted his report. This Court recorded the fact that the amount of Rs.250
crores have been received from the Appellant by the Respondent No.2. On
13.01.2026, this Court granted time to the parties to submit suggestions, if any,
to the report dated 09.07.2025 by Justice Anil R. Dave.
19. Both the Appellant and the Respondent Nos.2 have submitted their
suggestions to the report filed by Justice Anil R. Dave. On 07.10.2026, the
parties made elaborate submissions and on 09.10.2026, both parties filed their
written submissions and additional written submissions before this Court.

Page 14 of 31
20. Though the parties had advanced elaborate submissions before the High
Court in respect of various issues with regard to classification of the debt as
NPA and challenged the validity of the assignment in favour of the Respondent
No.2, before this Court, submissions were predominantly confined to the report
filed by Justice Anil R. Dave and as to the issue whether any sum is payable to
the assignee of the debt, namely, Respondent No.2 by the Appellant over and
above the sum of Rs.250 crores.
21. It is a fact that the issue as to classification of the asset as a Non-Performing Asset was done with effect from 16.10.2020 retrospectively by a
letter dated 31.03.2021 by the Respondent No.1. It is also not disputed that the
classification of term loan as NPA had been done irrespective of the fact that
there was a COVID-19 circular operating by the RBI by which the moratorium
period was extended up to 31.08.2020. The Respondent No.1 had revised the
term loan repayment schedule fixing the first instalment as 30.09.2020 and
subsequently monies have been received by the Respondent No.1 on
01.11.2020 and 11.12.2020.
22. It is relevant to point out that the Respondent No.1 after issuing a recall
notice of the loan on 17.01.2022, and after filing an application for recovery
before the DRT-I, Kolkata, also filed a petition under Section 7 of the IBC
before the NCLT seeking initiation of the CIRP against the Appellant. The said
application is still pending in the NCLT.

Page 15 of 31
23. Subsequently, the Respondent No.1 also issued a notice dated
08.07.2022 under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, recording the default
of the Appellant's account as NPA as on 16.10.2020 and demanded the
Appellant to pay a sum of Rs.410,26,78,340/- along with further interest,
incidental expenses and costs. On 28.10.2022, the Respondent No.1 issued a
notice under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, however, this was recalled
by a further notice dated 04.11.2022.
24. It is clear from the above that the Respondent No.1 has been initiating
proceedings in the DRT, NCLT and started the proceedings under the
SARFAESI Act, all simultaneously. Though this Court in the case of
Transcore v. Union of India and Another2 has held that the remedy under the
SARFAESI Act is treated as an additional remedy along with that contemplated
under the DRT Act and, therefore, withdrawal of an original application
pending before the DRT under the DRT Act is not a pre-condition for taking
recourse to the SARFAESI Act and it is for the bank or the financial institution
to exercise its discretion as to cases in which it may apply for leave and in cases
where it may not apply for leave to withdraw the DRT application before
proceeding under the SARFAESI Act.
2
(2008) 1 SCC 125

Page 16 of 31
25. This Court is also conscious of the judgment in ICICI Bank Limited v.
Official Liquidator of APS Star Industries Limited and Others3
, wherein it
has been held:-
"46. As stated above, an outstanding in the account of a borrower(s)
(customer) is a debt due and payable by the borrower(s) to the bank.
Secondly, the bank is the owner of such debt. Such debt is an asset in the
hands of the bank as a secured creditor or mortgagee or hypothecatee.
The bank can always transfer its asset. Such transfer in no manner affects
any right or interest of the borrower(s) (customer). Further, there is no
prohibition in the BR Act, 1949 in the bank transferring its assets inter
se. Even in the matter of assigning debts, it cannot be said that the banks
are trading in debts, as held by the High Court(s). The assignor Bank has
never purchased the debt(s). It has advanced loans against security as part
of its banking business. The account of a client in the books of the bank
becomes non-performing asset when the client fails to repay. In assigning
the debts with underlying security, the bank is only transferring its asset
and is not acquiring any rights of its client(s). The bank transfers its asset
for a particular agreed price and is no longer entitled to recover anything
from the borrower(s). The moment ICICI Bank Ltd. transfers the debt
with underlying security, the borrower(s) ceases to be the borrower(s) of
the ICICI Bank Ltd. and becomes the borrower(s) of Kotak Mahindra
Bank Ltd. (assignee)."
26. The Respondent No.2 has also relied upon a judgment of this Court in
Bijnor Urban Cooperative Bank Limited, Bijnor And Others v. Meenal
Aggarwal and Others4 wherein it was held that no writ of mandamus could be
issued by High Court under Article 226 directing a bank or a financial
institution to positively grant benefit of OTS to a borrower and it is always
3
(2010) 10 SCC 1
4
(2023) 2 SCC 805

Page 17 of 31
subject to eligibility criteria mentioned under the OTS scheme and guidelines
issued from time to time.
27. Be that as it may, the conduct of the Respondent No.1-bank in initiating
proceedings before the DRT and the NCLT and subsequently classifying the
assets as NPA with retrospective effect and issuing a notice under Section 13(2)
of the SARFAESI Act despite there being several communications between the
Appellant and Respondent No.1 regarding a proposed one time settlement and
the subsequent issue of notice under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act which
was withdrawn by a further notice dated 04.11.2022 subsequent to which an
OTS was proposed for a sum of Rs.238 crores on 07.02.2023. In fact, towards
this OTS the Appellant had paid about Rs.25 crores during the period of OTS
talks. Because of this the e-auction notice dated 10.02.2023 issued by the
Respondent No.1 placing the loan account for transfer to eligible asset
reconstruction companies, banks and financial institutions came as a bolt out of
the blue for the Appellant. The Appellant had challenged this notice dated
10.02.2023 by filing a WPO No.428 of 2023 before the High Court and by an
interim order dated 06.03.2023, the High Court deferred the e-auction. Since
there were talks between the parties, it appears that this writ petition was
withdrawn on 21.03.2023. However, on 23.03.2023 the Respondent No.1
issued a corrigendum advancing the e-auction process of the stressed loan
exposure to 24.03.2023. The Appellant immediately preferred WPO No.722

Page 18 of 31
of 2023 seeking cancellation of the web notice dated 10.02.2023, corrigendum
dated 23.03.2023 and also challenging the classification of its account as a Non-Performing Asset. The Appellant contended before the High Court that the
classification was contrary to the RBI's master circular on asset classification
and the COVID-19 relief circulars. Any default would have commenced only
from 01.12.2020 and without a valid classification, the loan could not have been
transferred as a stressed loan. While the Single Judge had allowed the writ
petition, the Division Bench, by the impugned judgment, has reversed the same.
PROCEEDINGS BEFORE HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ANIL R. DAVE: -
28. Pursuant to this Court's order dated 09.12.2024, Hon'ble Mr. Justice
Anil R. Dave, former Judge of this Court, issued notices to the parties on
25.12.2024 and held a preliminary meeting on 02.01.2025. Respondent No.1
did not take part and abstained during the course of the proceedings.
29. The hearing took place on 11.02.2025. The Appellant stated that it was
ready and willing to pay Rs. 250 crores, along with reasonable interest from the
date the Respondent No.2 had paid that amount to Respondent No.1.
Respondent No.2 disagreed, on the ground that Respondent No.1 had assigned
its rights to it and that it was entitled to act in pursuance of those rights. The
hearing before Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil R. Dave concluded on 06.03.2025, and
the parties were directed to place on record their short submissions.

Page 19 of 31
30. The Appellant inter alia submitted that the sum of Rs. 250 crores paid
by Respondent No.2 to Respondent No.1 was not its own money, but
Respondent No.2 was funded by CFMARC Vinimay Private Limited, which
was controlled by the Patwari Family. The Patwari family also held substantial
shares in Rashmi Metalics Limited, a competitor of the Appellant in the same
business. According to the Appellant, the Patwari Family orchestrated the
entire episode to take over its running business.
31. On the other hand, Respondent No.2 submitted that, as an assignee, it
was entitled to recover whatever amount the Appellant owed to Respondent
No.1, including interest and the penal interest. It further submitted that the 7.5%
offer was unreasonable, as the Appellant's dues already exceeded Rs. 250
Crores and therefore there is no question of the Appellant making payment of
Rs. 250 Crores to Respondent No 2. It was further submitted that, as on the date
of assignment of the debt by Respondent No. 1 in favour of Respondent No. 2,
Rs. 342 Crores was payable towards the principal amount, and interest thereon
was Rs. 112 Crores. The Appellant is therefore liable to pay the said amount,
to Respondent No.2 along with interest thereon, from the date on which the
debt was assigned to Respondent No. 2. It was also submitted that the manner
in which it funded the sum of Rs. 250 Crores was irrelevant to the Appellant's
liability. The relevant portions of the Report read as under: -
"28. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the Company submitted
that the Company has a right, as an assignee, to recover whatever amount,
the Petitioner had to pay to the Bank. Upon the assignment, all rights

Page 20 of 31
which the Bank had against the Petitioner, had been assigned to the
Company, and therefore the Company has to recover whatever amount
the Petitioner had to pay to the Bank, the principal amount and interest,
including the penal interest thereon.
30. According to him, the principal amount payable by the Petitioner to
the Bank as on 24 March 2023, as per the Assignment Agreement was
₹3,41,57,84,535/-. He submitted that the said amount being the principal
amount as on that date, the Petitioner is bound to pay interest thereon also.
In view of the said fact, the Company has rightly claimed a sum of ₹341
crores from the Petitioner. As a matter of fact, according to the learned
counsel, the Petitioner would be paying much less than what it was bound
to pay to the Bank, even if the Petitioner pays a sum of ₹341, crores to
the Company.
37. As the facts and circumstances of the case have already been narrated
in brief here in above, I need not repeat the same. Suffice is to state that
after hearing both sides and looking at the facts of the case, I have to
decide the amount which the Petitioner is liable to pay by way of interest
and/or any other amount over and above ₹250 crores to the Company.
